title: Me on the cyberattacks
content:
Tyler Cowen: Don’t Be Fooled By Randomness

The problems are serious, but the sky is not falling in. When it comes to the recent service outages, keep a few points in mind.

First, cyber risk is considerably higher than it used to be. Due to progress in AI systems, cyber offense has outraced cyber defense. Plenty of experts are attesting that a wide variety of systems can be hacked using advanced AI agents.

Second, not every reported incident is a cyberattack. In many cases we do not know, or somebody knows (one way or the other) and is not telling us. One possibility is that these are normal service outages but the world is paying more attention, so the number of problems appears to be spiraling out of control. Another is that institutions are patching or upgrading their systems to limit future cyberattacks, and something in the upgrade goes wrong, causing an outage.

For instance, Microsoft’s November 12 outage, the FAA’s November 13 ground stop, and JPMorgan Chase’s November 16 outage all seem to have been something other than direct cyberattacks.

Do not be too ready to look for patterns in the data, and recall the title of Nassim Taleb’s book: Fooled by Randomness.

Third, the risk of a larger and costlier AI-driven cyberattack remains real. The United States has redundancy and protective systems built into its national security establishment, its financial institutions, and its basic infrastructure. But those protections are imperfect, and with enough attempts somebody might break through and cause real damage.

We do need an emergency national emphasis on cyber defense, but in the meantime do not get carried away by anecdotes. Scrolling social media is not the best way to process this information. Instead, keep in mind that cybersecurity has been a big problem for a long time.

That is from a broader Free Press symposium.
